figures.caption: Fig. 1: Neural-DISCO overview. (a) Neural-DISCO reconstructs source spike counts from supervised label latents and a bottlenecked residual latent. (b) Counterfactual editing replaces a selected label latent while holding the remaining label blocks and the source residual fixed. (c) The same block-structured generator supports label-specific neuron attribution.

Fig. 2: Controlled RatInABox evaluation. (a) Simulated movement with place, head-direction and speed cells. (b) Cell-type recovery across λ; speed-cell recovery uses residual attribution because speed is withheld. (c) Residual PCA colored by speed. (d,e) Position shift while retaining head direction and speed. (f,g) Head-direction reversal while retaining position and speed. Generated neural activity is scored against simulator targets.

Fig. 3: Counterfactual editing in macaque reaching electrophysiology. (a) Editing replaces handposition, hand-velocity and eye-position blocks while retaining the source residual. (b) Trajectories decoded from source spikes, target spikes and Neural-DISCO counterfactual activity. (c,d) Synthetic constant-rate controls test whether attribution distinguishes recorded neurons from controls. (e) Target-decoding R2 comparisons; dotted lines show the empirical target-spike decoding reference.

Fig. 4: Allen Visual Coding evaluation. (a,g) Speed- and orientation-edit schematics. (b,c) Speed-edit example and speed-target RMSE. (d,e) Temporal-frequency preservation example and balanced accuracy after speed editing. (h,i) Orientation-edit example and target-orientation balanced accuracy. (j,k) Running-speed preservation example and speed RMSE after orientation editing. Editing summaries are mean ± SEM across 32 session means, each averaging ten folds. (f,l) Runningmodulation AUC and orientation-selectivity correlation across λ. In summary bars, Source denotes decoding of recorded activity.

Table 1: RatInABox editing against exact simulator target trajectories. Population R2 averages neuron-wise scores. All three populations are evaluated against simulator target rates in both edits. Values and joint scores are computed per fold and reported as mean ± SEM across ten folds. Each component is clipped before computing the edit–preservation score.

Table 2: Allen speed editing and temporal-frequency preservation across 32 sessions, using a common fold-training mean target. Metrics and SEP are computed per fold and averaged over ten folds within each session; values are mean ± SEM across the 32 session means. Lower speed RMSE and higher TF balanced accuracy and SEP are better.

Table 4: Orientation editing and source preservation across 32 Allen sessions. Metrics and SEP are computed per fold and averaged over ten folds within each session; values are mean ± SEM across the 32 session means. All methods share decoders trained on real fold-training activity and are evaluated on the same held-out presentations and targets. Speed RMSE measures error relative to source speed. Lower speed RMSE and higher balanced accuracy and SEP are better.

Table 5: Additional Allen stimulus edits in session 756029989. Values are mean ± SEM across ten folds, with E, P and SEP computed within each fold before aggregation. All methods share decoders trained on real fold-training activity and are evaluated on the same held-out presentations and targets. Higher values are better.

Table 13: Trainable parameter counts for the main editing models. Allen counts are shown for session 756029989 (672 units). The unregularized control (w/o reg.) has the same architecture as NeuralDISCO within each dataset and task and therefore has the same number of trainable parameters.
Fig. 5: Withheld-label diagnostics visualization. Across the three held-out-label settings, the residual latent is organized by the omitted variable and not by the observed variables.
Fig. 6: Withheld-label diagnostics decoding for Rat in a Box dataset. Residual-latent decoders recover the held-out variable much more strongly than the observed variables.

Fig. 7: Residual decoding with withheld factors on Allen. Each row withholds one factor from the model’s supplied variables; columns show how well each factor can be decoded from the residual latent. Chance is 0.125 for orientation, and 0.2 for temporal frequency. Each factor is more decodable when it is withheld, as reflected by the diagonal entries. The residual preferentially retains omittedfactor information, although some supplied-factor information remains (Table 6).

Fig. 9: RatInABox Attribution Heatmap. Rows correspond to neurons ordered by synthetic cell type: place cells, head-direction cells, and speed cells. Columns show normalized attribution to head-direction, position, and residual blocks. (a) Attribution results of Neural-DISCO. (b) Attribution results of architecture-matched unregularized residual control.

Fig. 10: RatInABox Counterfactual Rates. Example rates for one cell of each type in (a) the position-shift edit and (b) the head-direction edit. Generated rates are compared with simulator target rates for each population.

Fig. 11: RatInABox position-shift trajectory ablation. Decoded trajectories for the position-shift counterfactual are shown for the source activity, target trajectory, the regularized Neural-DISCO counterfactual, and the architecture-matched unregularized control. The regularized model tracks the shifted target manifold substantially better, whereas the unregularized control exhibits diffuse trajectories and poorer preservation of the intended edit.

Fig. 12: MC Maze decoding for the unregularized control. Downstream decodingR2 for generated activity from the architecture-matched unregularized control, evaluated against both the source and target trajectories. For all three observed factors, the unregularized control remains closer to the source than to the target, indicating that it fails to perform the intended counterfactual edit.

Fig. 13: MC Maze qualitative reach examples for the unregularized control. Example handposition trajectories for four source-target trial pairs. The generated counterfactual trajectories remain between the source and target reaches rather than matching the target movement, consistent with the poor target-decoding performance of the unregularized control.

Fig. 14: Allen Attribution Heatmap sorted by Orientation Selectivity Index. X-axis corresponds to individual units, with x-ticks indicating gOSI cutoffs, colored by orientation attribution value. Attribution scores are averaged over ten folds before min–max normalization within each method. (a) Attribution results of Neural-DISCO. (b) Attribution results of architecture-matched unregularized residual control.
